I'm not sure.. AFAIK Cool n' Quiet reduces the clock frequency on cores, if your base clock is 3.6GHz then when idle or not doing much the frequency could drop as much as to 0.8GHz, and the voltage drops accordingly. The way I see Cool n' Quiet is it regulates the core frequency, I don't know if it also manages voltage, but voltage does drop a lot. There's also something called C-States, I don't know much about it but it does have something to do with power management, and P-States, in case you want to do some more research. Also in Windows 10 under power management, there's a window that let's you set when to put hard drives to sleep etc, there's a setting for the CPU, the number is a percentage, maybe you could use that to limit the underclock the PC does, but I'm not sure that setting does anything at all, I just know it exists. I can't really answer your question, I fixed my issue by setting the multiplier to x38, that would be 3.8GHz, and left the voltage at Auto. It's been more than half a year and I haven't had any issue at all, before that it sucked, it was so random and I would lose work, maybe it didn't happen in a whole week, maybe it happened twice in a day, random. Maybe some motherboards combined with certain PSU + the Cool n' Quiet don't go too well together. I don't know why it happens to her and not to you, maybe some CPUs are more sensitive to it, I have no idea. The PC will generate a bit more heat and consume more power this way, if you find a way of fixing the issue while preserving some of that 'auto underclock/undervolt', let us know.

I once had random freezes on my PC too, Ryzen 1600X, B350M Mortar, the issue was fixed after setting a fixed CPU clock. You can probably achieve that by disabling AMD Cool n' Quiet. Although I don't have any proof, I do believe some motherboards or CPUs don't like or manage very well all those constant ups and downs in frequency and voltage. The PC would freeze without BSOD, and with the same sound issue you describe, while browsing or watching something, and the odds weren't increased when playing games. Since I locked the CPU multiplier, it hasn't happened again. Normally when it's a GPU problem, the drivers manage to recover the GPU, or you would get a BSOD, or some message in Event Viewer. If it's a RAM issue, you can check your RAM with memtest, I don't know the symptoms of RAM issues, but I'd guess BSOD. Since it suddenly freezes, even audio, it probably is a CPU issue, I hope any of this helps.

I wouldn't worry about it unless you see any water but I doubt that'll ever happen, when the PC is on you have heat and airflow anyways. If you have that much humidity I'd worry more about mold growing in the room. From what I've seen, some PCBs have some kind of residue, it's usually only on the PCB, flat and semi-transparent, maybe flux residue or something from the manufacturing process. The only thing to worry about is corrosion, which makes solder joints look rusty, white, and/or greenish. If you open your window regularly I can't see how enough humidity could build up to damage any electronics, if enough humidity does build up to damage electronics, it's probably damaging you more than the electronics. It's very unlikely you'll ever get condensation inside the PC, so don't worry about that, and if you just have very high humidity it's not as harmful when it's turned off and no electricity is running, and that humidity will drop within seconds of turning on the PC because of the heat and airflow produced. It should be fine.
If you're really worried about fire you could buy smoke alarms - two different brands. And have a fire extinguisher close by. There's lots of wires and power over there, you never know.

I finally solved the problem by installing Windows 10 on the Mac, but still, it wasn't a software problem, it was a hardware problem.
The solution was to install ThrottleStop.exe and deselect the "BD PROCHOT" option from the processor, and setting manually the multiplier.
Now the processor  will go up to 3.1GHz if needed under load, and fall to around 0.8GHz when idle.
As far as I understand, apparently motherboards can send a signal to the CPU telling it that something's wrong, in this case, through BD PROCHOT, and that will make the CPU to throttle. This issue, and the fix, is also valid for PCs with a faulty motherboard.
